scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a two-view response holding that technology can weaken or strengthen connection depending on use; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: We can now speak instantly with people across the world, yet often sit silently beside those next to us.
Some believe our growing use of technology reduces our chances for human interaction, while others believe it gives us better ways to connect.
I believe both views hold truth, and that technology can either weaken or strengthen our connections depending on how we use it.

sections.role: Body 1 — How technology can reduce interaction

sentences.text: First, technology really can reduce genuine human interaction.
People absorbed in their screens often ignore the family and friends right beside them.
For example, a group at dinner may each stare at a phone instead of talking to one another.
This shows that technology can pull us away from the people physically near us.
Online messages can also feel thin and cold compared with a real face-to-face conversation.
Spending hours alone with a device can leave people lonelier rather than closer.
To this extent, the first view captures a real danger.

sections.role: Body 2 — How technology can connect us

sentences.text: Second, however, technology also gives us powerful new ways to connect.
Phones and the internet let us stay close to people we could otherwise never reach.
Consider a family spread across distant countries who can now see and speak to one another every day.
Such connection shows that technology can bring people together across great distances.
Online communities also help lonely or isolated people find others who share their interests.
Used well, these tools can deepen relationships rather than replace them.
Both views, then, are true, depending on how the technology is used.
In conclusion, technology can indeed pull us away from the people around us.
But it can also connect us with others in valuable new ways.
Whether technology weakens or strengthens our bonds depends far less on the tools than on how we use them.
